extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers / experimental physicists studying motion in fluids (17th-century)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and theoretical rules for designing, conducting, and interpreting experiments and demonstrations about resistance, wave and pulse propagation, and sound in fluids, using pendulums, oscillating columns, and geometrical constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance ≈ proportional to square of velocity
rubrics_metrics.description: “resistentia augebatur in duplicata ratione velocitatis quamproxime.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pendulum experiments (measuring arcs and oscillation decay) to infer that the component of resistance varying with velocity is approximately proportional to the duplicate (square) ratio of velocity; note this is stated as an approximation and validated by multiple pendulum trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: At extreme speeds resistance may exceed square-law slightly
rubrics_metrics.description: “Debebit tamen resistentia tam in aere quam in aqua, si velocitas per gradus in infinitum augeatur, augeri tandem in ratione paulo plusquam duplicata ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize a caveat: for very large velocities the resistance eventually increases a little more than the duplicate ratio, due to effects (e.g., parts of the medium left as a near-vacuum) not captured by the approximate square law. Interpret high-speed data with caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance approximately proportional to fluid density
rubrics_metrics.description: From experiments: “resistentia argenti vivi ad resistentiam aquæ ut 13 vel 14 ad 1 ... id est ut densitas argenti vivi ad densitatem aquæ.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare identical bodies (spheres) oscillating in different fluids (mercury vs water) to infer that resistance scales roughly with the fluid's density. Control for sphere size and vessel geometry (avoid vessels too narrow). Prefer larger spheres and vessels to reduce confinement errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: External surface dominates resistance; internal contents negligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with a lead can (pyxis) shows internal parts contribute negligibly: internal resistance is thousands of times smaller (calculated A to B as 5928:1), concluding internal resistance is 'nulla aut plane insensibilis'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To test whether resistance arises from fluid entering internal pores, compare oscillation times of the same closed body when empty vs filled; ensure reliable suspension (firm hook) to avoid spurious elongation. Numerical comparison can quantify internal vs external contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure fluid resistance via pendulum amplitude decay
rubrics_metrics.description: Method: observe arc descents and ascents and number of oscillations; differences in successive arcs and oscillation counts give the resistance (table of arcs and oscillation numbers provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct pendulums with known geometry; record initial and final arc extents and count oscillations until given points. Use differences of arcs and counts to compute the portion of motion lost to resistance. Repeat trials and attend to experimental errors (e.g., suspension point stability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mechanical systematic errors (firm suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that when the hooking (uncus) was weak, measured retardation was larger because the hook yielded; remedy: make the hook firm so the suspension point remains fixed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the suspension mechanism is rigid and does not give under load, because yielding of support alters effective pendulum length and corrupts resistance measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure in a fluid does not propagate in straight lines unless particles are aligned
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLI: “Pressio non propagatur per Fluidum secundum lineas rectas, nisi ubi particulæ Fluidi in directum jacent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theoretical criterion for interpreting pressure transmission: when particles are not colinear, applied pressure spreads obliquely and divergently through the fluid; use this to reason about flow around obstacles and passage through apertures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motion through a fluid diverges from straight paths into surrounding still regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLII: motions propagated through a fluid diverge from the straight tract into spaces at rest (cases illustrated with water waves and pulses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect spreading (diffraction/divergence) of motion after passage through an aperture; experiments with water waves (surface undulations) or sound in rooms illustrate that transmitted motion dilates into surrounding still medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elastic vs non-elastic medium determines pulse geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLIII: “Corpus omne tremulum in Medio Elastico propagabit motum pulsuum undique in directum; in Medio vero non Elastico motum circularem excitabit.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret whether a trembling source produces straight-line pulses (elastic media) or circular/rotational displacements (non-elastic): this guides which observables (linear pulses, concentric wavefronts, or circulating flow) to expect in experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oscillating fluid columns are isochronous with suitably chosen pendulums
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLIV and corollaries: if water in two vertical legs alternately rises and falls and a pendulum is constructed with length equal to half the length of the water column, the water will rise and fall in the same times the pendulum oscillates; 'Isochonae' property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the pendulum–oscillating-column correspondence to time fluid reciprocations: choose pendulum length as prescribed (half the total column length) to get matching periods; useful for calibrating and measuring oscillation periods of fluid systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wave velocity related to wave latitude (wavelength) by a square-root relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLV/XLVI: 'Undarum velocitas est in dimidiata ratione latitudinum.' Construction: use a pendulum whose length equals the wave latitude; the wave's advance equals the pendulum's oscillation timings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine wave speed by relating the number of pendulum oscillations to how far a wave progresses: larger latitude (wavelength) implies different period; corollaries give numerical examples and scaling (velocity changes in the 'dimidiata'—square-root—ratio of latitude).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulse speed in an elastic fluid scales as sqrt(elasticity)/sqrt(density)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLVII: 'Pulsuum ... velocitates sunt in ratione composita ex dimidiata ratione vis Elasticæ directe & dimidiata ratione densitatis inverse', assuming elastic force proportional to condensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing media, compute pulse velocity from medium properties: increase in elastic restoring force raises speed (proportionally to the square root), increase in density lowers speed (inversely to the square root). Apply to sound/small-amplitude pulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluid particles in propagated pulses follow pendulum (harmonic) acceleration and retardation law
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLVIII: particles driven by pulses move reciprocally in very short motions, accelerating and retarding according to the law of an oscillating pendulum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model local particle motion in a pulse as small harmonic vibrations; this justifies using pendulum analogies to predict local accelerations, phases, and energy transfer in wave propagation experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure to compute pulse velocity from medium parameters using pendulum/cycloid construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. XLIX: give a construction: suppose medium compresses under a weight; take A as height whose weight equals the compressive weight, build a pendulum of length A, and the time for a full oscillation relates to pulse travel along a circumferential length of radius A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the geometric pendulum/cycloid analogy to derive pulse speed from given density and elasticity: construct the specified pendulum and compare oscillation period to the circumferential length that a pulse travels; follow the proposition's algebraic substitutions for practical calculation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure pulse (wavelength) distance by dividing traversable space by number of vibrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Prop. L: 'Datis Medii densitate & vi Elastica, invenire velocitatem pulsuum... Corporis ... inveniatur numerus Vibrationum dato tempore. Per numerum illum dividatur spatium quod pulsus eodem tempore percurrere possit, & pars inventa erit pulsus unius latitudo.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To find the distance (width) of one pulse: count the number of source vibrations in a given time and divide the total distance a pulse could traverse in that time by that number. Use precise counts of vibrations and reliable measure of pulse travel distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of sound: propagation by whole-air agitation; speed depends on air density
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholium: argument and computations concluding that 'soni ... in aeris totius agitatione consistat' and that sound speed depends on the total air density (examples with densities of mercury and air, pendulum-derived estimates of sound speed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or interpreting acoustic experiments, treat sound as longitudinal pulses in the air whose speed is determined by air's density and elasticity; compare theoretical estimates (via pendulum constructions and known densities) with empirical echo/observation data, and be aware of experimental variability.
